summary: Cape Breton light on the eastern end of Fourchu Head, first shown 1907-08. Its keepers left in 1988; the Coast Guard runs it, and a skeletal tower replaced the fibreglass one in 2015.

structures.note: Replaced the fibreglass tower, per Lighthouse Friends.
32 ft (9.8 m) per NSLPS. Lighthouse Friends dates the fibreglass tower to 1979, and says it replaced the traditional lighthouse.
First tower, 32 ft (9.8 m) to the top of the ventilator (Department, 1908); replaced by the fibreglass tower.

access.note: Reached by the road east from Fourchu to its end, then across the breakwater (Lighthouse Friends). NSLPS: requires a hike.

events.note: NSLPS and the record: 1907. Lighthouse Friends: announced complete in 1908. The Department lists the light among those erected in 1907-8, the year to 31 March 1908.
Albert Hooper appointed first keeper, 18 May 1908.
Fixed red dioptric light, given as sixth order in the narrative and as 5th order French lens in the list of new lights. The sources differ.
Struck a ledge off Fourchu on 23 February 1921; the Department's inquiry refers to the non-existence of light on Fourchu Head and cautioned the master. The vessel is not named in the text read.
Sixth-order dioptric lens, fixed red, seasonal (April to January), 1922-1943 (NSLPS).
Tower rebuilt August-September 1950 while a temporary light was shown from the oil shed roof (Lighthouse Friends).
NSLPS: fog signal established 1955. Lighthouse Friends: fog alarm building with diaphone built 1956.
The Souris, P.E.I., dragger Iceland II wrecked near Fourchu Head in late February 1967; ten men died. Staff at the light helped the search.
Electronic foghorn placed in operation (Lighthouse Friends).
Round fibreglass tower with beacon replaced the traditional lighthouse (Lighthouse Friends). NSLPS dates the fibreglass tower to 1985.
NSLPS: fibreglass tower replaced the original 1907 tower.
Last keeper, Robert Spears, left in 1988 (Lighthouse Friends); NSLPS: automated by 1988.
Coast Guard put up a galvanized square skeletal tower to replace the fibreglass tower; the characteristic remained the same (Lighthouse Friends).
Coast Guard discontinued the fog signal; announced in May 2015 and silenced afterwards (Lighthouse Friends).

wrecks.vessel: not named in the text read
wrecks.outcome: Struck a ledge off Fourchu, Cape Breton. Ice pressure carried her inshore in weather and darkness. The inquiry's view was that the master would not have struck had he known there was no light on Fourchu Head; he was cautioned.

wrecks.vessel: Iceland II (Souris, P.E.I., steel stern dragger)
wrecks.outcome: Wrecked in a storm near Fourchu Head; no survivors; ten men died. Staff at the light relayed radio-telephone messages for the search and recovered two bodies.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record's 1907 (Rowlett, NSLPS) and Lighthouse Friends' 1908 (the Department's announcement) both fit: the Department lists Fourchu Head among lights erected in the fiscal year to 31 March 1908, which began in April 1907. The first keeper was appointed 18 May 1908.

The record's LFl W 6s is the Coast Guard's current characteristic. The fixed red light of 1908 and 1922-1943 (NSLPS) is an earlier one, and NSLPS dates the white fixed light to 1992. The record's OSM value 'F W' is not checked here.

The record's 1985 tower is the fibreglass tower of NSLPS and Wikidata. Lighthouse Friends says it was replaced in 2015. The first tower of 1907-08 was wooden, square, with a sloping-sided body and a square lantern (Department, 1908).

notes_for_editor: 1) Fourchu Head (Richmond County) is not Cape Forchu or Cape Fourchu near Yarmouth. The Department's reports of 1900-1924 carry many Yarmouth 'Cape Fourchu' entries (lights, fog alarms, a 1908 keeper, Thomas Doane); none is used here. 2) Albert Hooper's salary: Lighthouse Friends gives $120 a year, and the 1910 staff table (scan 167) gives $150 in the same row; salary is left out. The table is OCR text with columns printed in blocks, so Hooper's row was matched to the station by position (the 1909 volume, scan 187, has 'Fourche Head Light' in the station column). The scan 167 page image was checked: the row reads Fourche Head, Light / Albert Hooper / May 18, 1908 / 150 00, so the staff table's salary is $150 and Lighthouse Friends' $120 stays unresolved (salary is not in the story). Scan 187 gives only a station list and is not used for names. 3) Lens order: the narrative (scan 74) says sixth-order dioptric; the list (scan 96) says 5th order French lens. Both are in the same report and the story leaves it open. 4) The Iceland II sailing and wreck dates: Lighthouse Friends gives 15 January 1967 as the sailing date and says the storm came five days after 17 February. A PEI climate blog gives 22 February for the departure and 23 February for the wreck; it was not read as a source here. Nauticapedia returned 403 and the CBC article timed out, so neither was read. Cape Breton's Magazine (Issue 31, 1982) carries a witness account of the wreck; it is not used (unnamed witness, copyrighted text). 5) The 1921 wreck's vessel name is not in the OCR passage read (scan 71). 6) A 1953 dory attack by a shark 'off Fourchu Head' appears in Lighthouse Friends' notes with no source; not used, a lead for a newspaper search. 7) The fibreglass tower year (1979 per Lighthouse Friends, 1985 per NSLPS and the record) is unresolved. 8) Wikipedia's 'established in 1907' was not cited. 9) A 1911 Kennebec Journal item on a derelict vessel 'reported by fishermen returning to Fourchu' is not tied to the light and is not used.
